{{short description|German mathematician}}
{{Expand German|topic=bio|Carl Hierholzer|date=December 2009}}
'''Carl Hierholzer''' (2 October 1840 – 13 September 1871<ref name="Hierholzer1873">{{cite journal|last=Hierholzer|first=Carl|author2=Chr. Wiener|title=Ueber die Möglichkeit, einen Linienzug ohne Wiederholung und ohne Unterbrechung zu umfahren |journal=Mathematische Annalen |year=1873 |volume=6|pages=30&ndash;32 |url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?PPN=GDZPPN002242176&IDDOC=38664 |accessdate=17 August 2012 |language=German |doi=10.1007/bf01442866|s2cid=119885172}}</ref>) was a [[Germans|German]] [[mathematician]].

==Biography==
Hierholzer studied mathematics in [[Universität Karlsruhe (TH)|Polytechnic School in Karlsruhe]], and he got his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Ruprecht-Karls-Universität Heidelberg]] in 1865. His Ph.D. advisor was [[Ludwig Otto Hesse]] (1811–1874). In 1870 Hierholzer wrote his [[habilitation]] about [[conic section]]s (title: ''Ueber Kegelschnitte im Raum'') in Karlsruhe, where he later became a [[Privatdozent]].

Hierholzer [[mathematical proof|proved]] that a [[connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] has an [[Eulerian trail]] if and only if exactly zero or two of its vertices have an odd [[degree (graph theory)|degree]]. This result had been given, with no proof of the 'if' part, by [[Leonhard Euler]] in 1736. Hierholzer apparently presented his work to a circle of fellow mathematicians not long before his premature death in 1871. A colleague  then arranged for its posthumous publication in a paper that appeared in 1873.<ref name="Hierholzer1873" />
